What comes up in Thirroul

3 conditions, and each one is handled differently

Every site is scoped on the day. The table describes how these jobs generally go in this area. Your block may not match it, which is the reason for looking at it first.

Benched cut on a steep coastal block

The characteristic Thirroul job, where the ground falls away faster than the street suggests.

How it is handled
Cut in benches from the high side with each level stable before the next, and the batter or retaining designed before the face is opened.
What does it
Tracked excavator able to work on a grade, tippers staged at the street.

Knockdown with restricted street access

Where the frontage and the gradient rule out the vehicles that would normally do the work.

How it is handled
Material walked down or carried out and loaded at the street in sequenced loads.
What does it
Mini and midi excavators, bogie or 10 wheeler tippers.

Freestanding houses

Single and double storey brick, brick veneer, fibro and timber. The era matters more than the material, because anything built before 1990 carries a hazardous materials assumption until it is tested.

How it is handled
Hazardous materials removed and cleared first, services disconnected in writing, then the structure taken down and the material separated as it falls.
What does it
Excavator with a demolition grapple, sized to the side access rather than to the house. Zero tail swing where the work runs hard against a boundary.

Thirroul

What shapes the work on these blocks

  • Steep blocks between escarpment and sea The defining constraint. The fall decides the volume, the batter and where plant can stand.
  • A narrow coastal strip Which limits where material can go and how it gets there.
  • Older coastal housing Weathered fibro and cement sheet across much of the pre 1990 stock.
  • Narrow streets Where truck standing frequently decides the vehicle and the load count.

Thirroul access is the hard part. Steep driveways, stepped frontages and narrow streets often mean a smaller machine working for longer with tippers staged at the street rather than at the work face. It is worked out before the quote, not on day one.

Thirroul questions

What people ask before we start

Can a machine get onto a steep block?
Usually, but what size decides the programme. A block that only takes a mini excavator takes longer and costs more per cubic metre than the same volume on an open site, and that is the first thing we look at.
Do you do the retaining?
The excavation, the benching and the preparation are ours. Structural retaining is designed by an engineer and built by a specialist, and the dig is planned around that design.
Do the steep blocks under the escarpment change the method?
Yes. A cut is taken in benches from the high side with each level stable before the next, machines have to be able to work on a grade, and tippers are usually staged at the street rather than at the work face.
Is Max licensed for the asbestos removal itself?
Max holds the demolition licence, AD214737. The asbestos removal is carried out by licensed asbestos removalists, and the air monitoring and clearance by an independent licensed assessor. The whole pathway is managed as one job so you are not coordinating three contractors.
